editorial.headline: Vegetable Retail: Nationally Open, but Not Registrable as PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Specialised vegetable retail is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium bars PMA registration today.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this specialised vegetable-retail activity as PMA in Bali today, even though the national record sets the foreign-ownership ceiling at 100%. That distinction is the point of the entry. National openness does not translate into current PMA registrability on the island. The activity itself is tightly legible: the specialised retail sale of vegetables, including shallots, garlic, potatoes, carrots, aubergines, beans, cucumbers, chayote, long beans and kidney beans. Those examples explain the commodity focus in plain commercial terms. What is being registered is a specialised retail activity centred on vegetables.

The registration field is not confined to one business size. The available scales run from Mikro and Kecil through Menengah and Besar—micro, small, medium and large. In practical terms, the record places the same activity within each of those named scale categories; the registrant is a business carrying out specialised vegetable retail. The size classification changes neither the listed vegetable focus nor the national-Bali distinction that follows. Each scale is expressly named in the record, so the activity’s availability across those sizes is clear.

At national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA: open. The 100% ceiling means the record permits complete foreign ownership nationally. This must be read as a national position, rather than a promise of registrability everywhere. That ceiling is a national PMA setting, not a Bali condition, and the two must be kept separate. The source named for the national position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For an investor considering the activity, the national answer is therefore direct: it is open to PMA up to the stated full foreign-ownership ceiling.

Bali produces a different result. The record says that at the Besar scale, OSS risk across every scope is Low/Medium-Low. Bali’s rule is permanent and island-wide: its moratorium blocks PMA registration at Low and Medium-Low risk. The resulting restriction is recorded as a Bali moratorium of May thirteenth, twenty twenty-six, with Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP identified as its source. The conclusion for foreign registration is direct. Despite national openness and a 100% national ceiling, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA in Bali today. The national and Bali positions are both material: one records national PMA openness; the other blocks the Bali registration.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness does not translate into current PMA registrability on the island.
